narrative: Fire ecology featured heavily this week, from early post-fire mammal declines in a Namibian tree-and-shrub savanna to evidence that nineteenth-century industrialisation drove an extreme pulse in Appalachian fire activity, while a Functional Ecology study linked serotiny in Pinus yunnanensis to local fire frequency. Climate-related work highlighted how strategic dam management can offset climate-driven declines in Yellowstone cutthroat trout productivity, and a Global Change Biology paper warned that weak experimental designs are widely underestimating drought impacts on river ecosystems. In behavioural ecology, free-ranging lizards were shown to actively regulate ultraviolet exposure independent of thermoregulation, while a landscape-scale hedgehog tracking study found that barrier-aware movement models outperform traditional geometric home-range estimators in cities. Population and trophic studies ranged from post-fire seed and microsite effects on seedling recruitment to a 24-year record of climate-driven shifts in owl-prey interactions in a semi-arid Chilean ecosystem. Invasion and community themes were well represented, including a global assessment of the ecological footprint of invasive freshwater fish and evidence that reduced litter allelochemicals can foster positive interactions among co-occurring alien species. On the methods and evolution fronts, new eDNA and remote-sensing tools continue to proliferate, from a combined eDNA-graph-theory-niche-modelling framework for ecosystem assessment to genomic evidence for post-glacial divergence between Australian and Cape fur seal subspecies.
